newsitem.title: GERMANY: Compuserve porn case may turn on German law.
newsitem.headline: Compuserve porn case may turn on German law.

text.p: A German Internet bill due to come up for a parliamentary vote in the next two weeks could undermine controversial pornography charges against a local CompuServe Corp executive, the man's lawyer said.

Under the Information and Communications Services Law, which already has the governing coalition's approval, Internet access providers generally would not be held liable for child pornography or other banned material on the Internet.

If the multimedia law takes effect on August 1 as scheduled, it could clear former CompuServe German chief Felix Somm of allowing the online service to make child pornography accessible in Germany, said Hans-Werner Moritz, his lawyer.
"This would clearly prevent any criminal liability, if the law comes through," Moritz told Reuters. "This would be good news for Felix Somm."

A spokesman for the Bavarian state prosecutor's office, which filed the charges against Somm in April, declined to discuss the CompuServe case but confirmed that changes in law often favour the accused in Germany.
"If you have a certain law at the time an act is committed, and during the process the law changes, it is always the law that is best for the accused person that counts," he said.

But another lawyer, Michael Schneider, who is familiar with Internet cases and who testified in parliament about the new law, said the impact would not be so clear. "If you argue it dogmatically, (the new law) should have no effect," Schneider said in Bonn.
A CompuServe spokeswoman said the company did not know what effect the new law would have. "It's speculation at this point," said Doris Kretzen in Munich.
The case against Somm, who said last week he would leave CompuServe to start his own business, is awaiting a court ruling on whether the prosecutor has grounds to take the indictments further.

The court has given no date for a decision, although Moritz said the court was waiting for the defence to present its position on the charges. Moritz expected to present the statement sometime in the next several weeks.
In the meantime, the case could take a decisive turn if the lower house of Germany's parliament passes the multimedia law, as expected.
"We feel very confident the law will pass," said Klaus Rupf, deputy secretary in the Ministry of Education, Science, Research and Technology in Bonn.
The law would require online services that provide content as well as access to the Internet to take reasonable measures to block material banned in Germany.
Companies that only provide access to the Internet would not be held liable for illegal content on computers in other countries, Moritz said.
The law would clear Somm because CompuServe GmbH was a separate company from parent CompuServe Corp and only provided access to the parent's content and the Internet, Moritz said.
"The GmbH is a pure access provider," he said.
After a year-long investigation, Somm was charged with distributing child pornography, Nazi writings and other banned materials via the Internet.
The prosecutor said Somm knowingly allowed the materials to be available in Germany through CompuServe.
CompuServe has called the charges "entirely baseless," and said last week it would continue to pay Somm's legal fees even though he planned to leave the firm.
Kretzen said Somm's departure was unrelated to the case against him. It was not known where or when Somm would start his company, or when his last day at CompuServe would be, she said.
The charges arrived in April after prosecutors said in January that they would take no action after a year-long investigation.
German authorities have also investigated Internet access provider EUnet Deutschland GmbH and America Online Inc.'s venture in Germany, AOL Bertelsmann GmbH, although neither firm was been charged.
